title: Undefined Behavior and Object Lifetime
summary: The compiler optimizes on the assumption that your program has **no undefined behaviour**. Break that assumption and it may delete checks, reorder code, or mis-compile something far from the fault. This lesson is the full catalogue, the rules of object lifetime, and the tools that keep you inside the lines.
markdown:
## Why it is worse than a crash [[1.10 Compiler Settings, Build Configurations and Undefined Behavior]] described undefined behaviour as "the rules say nothing about what happens". The practical consequence is sharper: an optimizer is entitled to assume it **never** happens, and to reason from that. ```cpp int table[4]{}; bool exists(int value) { for (int i{ 0 }; i <= 4; ++i) // off by one: reads table[4] { if (table[i] == value) { return true; } } return false; } ``` Reading `table[4]` is undefined. So a conforming optimizer may conclude that the loop must return before `i` reaches 4, which means it always returns `true`, and compile the whole function to `return true;`. Real compilers have done exactly this. ```cpp void check(int* p) { const int x{ *p }; // dereferenced: so the compiler may assume p is not null if (p == nullptr) // therefore this test is "always false" and is removed { return; } use(x); } ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR A["The code contains
undefined behaviour"] --> B["The optimizer assumes
it cannot occur"] B --> C["It derives facts that
are false at run time"] C --> D["Checks are deleted and code reordered,
often far from the original fault"] ``` Two properties make it treacherous. The effect can appear **before** the offending operation executes, because the whole function was compiled under the false assumption. And it changes with optimization level, compiler version and unrelated edits. ## The catalogue | Category | Examples | |---|---| | **Arithmetic** | Signed integer overflow; division by zero; shifting by a negative amount or by the width of the type or more; `INT_MIN / -1` | | **Memory** | Out-of-bounds access; dereferencing null; use after free; double delete; mismatched `new[]` and `delete` | | **Lifetime** | Dangling references and pointers; returning a reference to a local; using an object after its destructor has run | | **Initialization** | Reading an uninitialized variable | | **Type punning** | Accessing an object through a pointer to an unrelated type; reading the inactive member of a union | | **Concurrency** | Data races | | **Library preconditions** | `v[v.size()]`; `front()` on an empty container; a comparator for `std::sort` that is not a consistent ordering; modifying a key in a `std::set` | | **Others** | Flowing off the end of a non-`void` function; modifying a `const` object; violating the One Definition Rule | The standard distinguishes three weaker cousins: | Term | Meaning | Example | |---|---|---| | **Implementation-defined** | The compiler chooses and documents it | `sizeof(int)` | | **Unspecified** | One of several allowed results, undocumented | The order in which function arguments are evaluated | | **Erroneous** (C++26) | Wrong, but with bounded, defined consequences | Reading an uninitialized local, from C++26 | ## Strict aliasing and type punning The **strict aliasing rule**: an object may be accessed only through an expression of its own type (with a few allowances for `const`, signedness and base classes). It lets the compiler assume that a `float*` and an `int*` never refer to the same memory, which enables important optimizations. ```cpp float f{ 1.0f }; std::uint32_t bad{ *reinterpret_cast(&f) }; // undefined: aliasing violation std::uint32_t good{ std::bit_cast(f) }; // defined, and constexpr std::uint32_t older{}; std::memcpy(&older, &f, sizeof older); // the pre-C++20 way ``` Reinterpreting the bits of one type as another is **type punning**. `std::bit_cast` and `std::memcpy` both copy the representation into a fresh object of the target type, and compilers turn either into a single move instruction. One exception is always allowed: any object's bytes may be examined through a pointer to `char`, `unsigned char` or `std::byte`. ## Object lifetime Memory existing is not the same as an object existing. ``` storage obtained ─▶ [ lifetime: initialization complete ... destructor begins ] ─▶ storage released ▲ the object may be used only inside this window ▲ ``` | Event | Lifetime | |---|---| | Storage is obtained, and initialization finishes | Begins | | The destructor starts, or the storage is released or reused | Ends | Using an object outside its lifetime is undefined, even when the bytes are still there and look intact. You can control the two halves separately: ```cpp alignas(Widget) std::byte buffer[sizeof(Widget)]; Widget* w{ std::construct_at(reinterpret_cast(buffer), arguments) }; // lifetime begins std::destroy_at(w); // lifetime ends ``` | Facility | Purpose | |---|---| | `std::construct_at`, `std::destroy_at` | Begin and end a lifetime in existing storage: [[13.03 Custom Memory Placement new, Allocators and PMR]] | | Implicit-lifetime types | Simple types (scalars, trivial structs, arrays of them) come into existence in storage from `malloc` or after a `memcpy` without explicit construction | | `std::start_lifetime_as(p)` (C++23) | Declares that bytes received from a file or the network are a `T` | | `std::launder` | Obtains a usable pointer in rare cases where storage is reused for an object with `const` or reference members | ## Temporaries A temporary lives until the end of the full expression that created it. One rule extends that: binding a temporary **directly** to a `const` reference (or an rvalue reference) keeps it alive as long as the reference. | Code | Result | |---|---| | `const std::string& r{ std::string{ "hi" } };` | Fine: the lifetime is extended to that of `r` | | `std::string_view sv{ std::string{ "temp" } };` | Dangles at the end of the statement: a view is not a reference binding | | `auto& first{ std::vector{ 1, 2, 3 }[0] };` | Dangles: the reference binds to an element, not to the temporary | | `const auto& n{ makePlayer().name() };` | Dangles if `name()` returns a reference into the temporary | Extension applies only to the temporary itself, not to things reached through it. ## Defences | Tool | Catches | |---|---| | AddressSanitizer | Out-of-bounds access, use after free, leaks | | UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer | Overflow, invalid shifts, null dereference, misalignment | | ThreadSanitizer | Data races | | Constant evaluation | The compiler **rejects** undefined behaviour inside a `constexpr` evaluation: [[11.04 Compile-Time Programming — constexpr, consteval, constinit]] | | A hardened standard library | Bounds checks on `operator[]`, `front()` and iterators. Xenon's Debug build has these on. | | Warnings and static analysis | Many patterns, before the program runs: [[13.09 Testing, Sanitizers, Static Analysis and Tooling]] | No tool finds everything. The durable defence is habit: prefer the constructs that cannot go wrong (`std::vector::at`, ranges, smart pointers, `std::bit_cast`, RAII), so that the dangerous ones are rare and visible. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? Why can undefined behaviour affect code that runs *before* the faulty operation? - Because the program runs its lines in a random order - Because the processor predicts the error in advance + The optimizer assumes the undefined behaviour never happens - It cannot; only later code is affected > The compiler reasons "this path would be UB, so it cannot happen" and may remove or rearrange earlier code on that basis. ? What is the safe way to reinterpret a `float`'s bits as an integer? - `*reinterpret_cast(&f)` - `static_cast(f)` - Write the `float` into a union and read the integer member + `std::bit_cast(f)`, or `std::memcpy` before C++20 > `reinterpret_cast` through a pointer breaks strict aliasing and the union trick is UB in C++. `static_cast` converts the value, not the bits. ? What does the strict aliasing rule allow the compiler to assume? + That pointers to unrelated types do not refer to the same object - That no two pointers ever hold the same address - That every pointer is non-null - That `char` pointers never alias anything > A write through a `float*` cannot change an `int`, so the compiler may keep the `int` in a register. (`char` and `std::byte` are the exceptions that may alias anything.) ? When does a temporary's lifetime get extended? - Whenever it is assigned to a variable - When it is passed to a function by value + When it is bound directly to a `const` reference or an rvalue reference - Never; temporaries always die at the end of the statement > It then lives as long as that reference. Binding through a function's returned reference does not extend it. ```
ideas:
1. Write six small functions, each containing one item from the catalogue. Then write the corrected version of each.
2. Put one in a `constexpr` function evaluated by a `static_assert` and read the compiler's diagnosis.
3. Predict which lines of the temporaries table dangle before looking at the answers.

cards.q: Why can undefined behaviour affect code that runs *before* the faulty operation?
cards.a:
The optimizer assumes the undefined behaviour never happens

The compiler reasons "this path would be UB, so it cannot happen" and may remove or rearrange earlier code on that basis.

cards.q: What is the safe way to reinterpret a `float`'s bits as an integer?
cards.a:
`std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t>(f)`, or `std::memcpy` before C++20

`reinterpret_cast` through a pointer breaks strict aliasing and the union trick is UB in C++. `static_cast` converts the value, not the bits.

cards.q: What does the strict aliasing rule allow the compiler to assume?
cards.a:
That pointers to unrelated types do not refer to the same object

A write through a `float*` cannot change an `int`, so the compiler may keep the `int` in a register. (`char` and `std::byte` are the exceptions that may alias anything.)

cards.q: When does a temporary's lifetime get extended?
cards.a:
When it is bound directly to a `const` reference or an rvalue reference

It then lives as long as that reference. Binding through a function's returned reference does not extend it.
